newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's Lebed sure of winning early election.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Lebed sure of winning early election.

text.p: Outspoken general Alexander Lebed, seen by some experts as Russia's next leader, said on Sunday he had no doubts an early election would be called because of President Boris Yeltsin's ill health and he would win it.
"I want to be president and I will be president," Lebed said in an interview with Russia's Channel Six television.
Asked if he was sure an early election would be called because of Yeltsin's poor health and whether he was ready to take part and win, Lebed answered "yes" .
The 46-year-old retired paratroop general dismissed the possibility of the election taking place as scheduled in the year 2000.
Yeltsin was admitted to hospital with pneumonia last Wednesday, only two weeks after his return to the Kremlin and two months after his quintuple bypass on November 5.
"Ill health is a personal drama, but this personal drama has been turned into a tragedy for the whole country," Lebed said.
"For half a year we watch this spectacle -- moves from a sanatorium to (the country residence of) Barvikha, then to the Central Clinical Hospital, then elsewhere.

"And there is no management of the country while all types of crises unfold in Russia...Only tough and serious management ...may help resolve the situation. A social explosion is another alternative."
Lebed finished a strong third in the first round of the presidential election last June and was immediately drafted by Yeltsin as Russia's national security chief.

Yeltsin allowed Lebed to sign a peace deal with Chechen separatists which the opposition blasted as surrender but which boosted Lebed's popularity because it put an end to a conflict in which tens of thousands have been killed.
Yeltsin even hinted at the time he might consider Lebed his future successor.
The appointment helped Yeltsin defeat communist Gennady Zyuganov in the run-off on July 3, but the Yeltsin-Lebed alliance lasted only until October 17.
Yeltsin, who was preparing for his heart operation at the time, dramatically went on television to sack Lebed, signing an order for his dismissal in front of the cameras.
He accused Lebed of failing as a team player and of manifesting overt presidential ambitions.

Lebed tops most latest opinion polls and most experts agree he is likely to be a frontrunner if a presidential election is held shortly. His chances are not so bright, they say, if the election is held in the year 2000 as scheduled.

After his dismissal Lebed outraged the Kremlin by his public alliance with the hawkish general Alexander Korzhakov, sacked by Yeltsin last June as his chief bodyguard despite a close personal friendship.
On Sunday, Lebed defended his alliance with Korzhakov, saying bluntly: "Enemies of my enemies are my friends."
In recent months Lebed has been busy forming his own political movement which he sees as a "third way" for Russia and which he intends to use as a springboad in a future election.
He said on television the movement, including chess champion Garyy Kasparov, was in a position immediately to raise enough funding to run a full-fledged campaign.
